_note: SYNTHETIC DEMO DATA — fixed questions and a keyword rubric so DEMO_MODE runs offline. The keyword scorer is a demo stand-in for the LLM grader, not a validated assessment. Bank entries apply ONLY to the demo project P01; transfer questions carry a scenario-specific rubric whose 'required' point is the conclusion the changed condition calls for.

D01.why: Why did the team remove duplicate images and impute missing labels before training, instead of training on the raw data?
D01.what_if: What if the team had kept the 310 duplicate images? What would happen to the reported test F1, and why?

transfer.prompt: Imagine a new batch where the same patient appears in several images. How would you split or clean the data, and why?
transfer.scenario: The same patient now appears in several images.

rubric.point: Split by patient, so all images of one patient stay in the same subset
Otherwise the same patient is seen in training and test (leakage)
Leakage would make the test scores look better than they really are

transfer.prompt: What if half of the missing labels could not be recovered from the radiologist's notes? What would you do with those images, and why?
transfer.scenario: Half of the missing labels cannot be recovered from the radiologist's notes.

rubric.point: Do not guess labels: drop those images or have an expert relabel them
Guessed labels would add label noise and a wrong training signal
Check that dropping them does not change the class balance or remove many positives

D01.hint: Think about what the model is allowed to see before it is tested.

rubric.point: Duplicates can leak between the training and test sets
keywords: both the training and the test

rubric.point: Leakage inflates the scores (over-optimistic results)
Imputing labels from radiologist notes keeps usable images

D02.why: Why did the team use Random Forest instead of Logistic Regression as the baseline?
D02.what_if: What if the hospital required that every prediction be easy to explain to a doctor? Would the Random Forest choice still hold? Why?

transfer.prompt: What if the features were already engineered so that the two classes were almost linearly separable? Which baseline would you pick now, and why?
transfer.scenario: The features are already almost linearly separable.

rubric.point: Logistic Regression becomes the better first baseline
A linear boundary is enough, so Random Forest's non-linearity adds little
Logistic Regression is faster and easier to interpret

transfer.prompt: What if training time had to stay under one second on a laptop? Would you still start from Random Forest? Why?
transfer.scenario: Training must take under one second on a laptop.

rubric.point: Start from Logistic Regression or a much smaller, faster model
A Random Forest with many trees is slower to train
Tradeoff: some F1 may be lost in exchange for speed

D02.hint: Think about what kind of relationships each model can represent.

rubric.point: Random Forest captures non-linear interactions between features
No manual feature engineering needed
Tradeoff: Logistic Regression is faster/more interpretable but scored lower

D03.why: Why did the team report F1 instead of accuracy as the headline metric?
D03.what_if: What if the dataset were balanced, with 50% of images showing a finding? Would F1 still be clearly better than accuracy? Why?

transfer.prompt: What if missing a finding (a false negative) became 10 times more costly than a false alarm? Which metric would you report, and why?
transfer.scenario: A false negative becomes 10 times more costly than a false alarm.

rubric.point: Prioritise recall: report recall or a recall-weighted metric such as F2
Accuracy stays misleading because of the class imbalance
Tradeoff: accept more false alarms in order to miss fewer findings

transfer.prompt: What if the test set contained only 2% positive images? How would that change what accuracy and F1 tell you?
transfer.scenario: Only 2% of the test images are positive.

rubric.point: Accuracy becomes even more misleading: always predicting 'no finding' gives about 98%
F1 still shows how well the rare positive cases are found (precision and recall)
With so few positives, the test F1 is noisy and needs enough positive cases

D03.hint: Think about what the share of 'finding' images does to each metric.

rubric.point: Class imbalance: only about 12% of images show a finding
Accuracy is misleading: always predicting 'no finding' gives about 88%
F1 is built on precision and recall of the positive class

D04.why: Why did the team use a stratified train/validation/test split instead of a purely random split?
D04.what_if: What if the dataset had 50,000 images instead of 4,200? Would stratification still matter as much? Why?

transfer.prompt: What if you had to use 5-fold cross-validation instead of one fixed split? What would you do about the folds, and why?
transfer.scenario: 5-fold cross-validation replaces the single fixed split.

rubric.point: Use stratified folds, so every fold keeps the share of positive images
Unstratified folds could get very few positives by chance
So the per-fold F1 would vary a lot and be unreliable

transfer.prompt: What if a new test set had to be only 100 images? How would you build it, and why?
transfer.scenario: The new test set may contain only 100 images.

rubric.point: Stratify the sample so it still holds about 12 positive images
A random 100-image sample could contain very few positives
F1 on 100 images is noisy, so report the uncertainty

D04.hint: Think about how many positive images end up in a small test set.

rubric.point: Stratification keeps the same share of positives in every subset
A random split could leave a small test set with very few positives
Otherwise the F1 estimate is unstable/unreliable

D05.why: Why did the team report that the model was not tested on images from other hospitals?
D05.what_if: What if another hospital wanted to use the model tomorrow? What would you tell them, and why?

transfer.prompt: What if a second hospital's images gave F1 = 0.50? How would you explain the drop, and what would you do next?
transfer.scenario: A second hospital's images give F1 = 0.50.

rubric.point: Explain the drop as a distribution (domain) shift between hospitals
The original test set came from the same single hospital, so it overestimated real-world performance
Next step: validate, fine-tune or retrain with data from the new hospital before use

transfer.prompt: What if the same hospital bought a new scanner? Would you trust the model on the new images? Why?
transfer.scenario: The same hospital buys a new scanner.

rubric.point: Do not trust it automatically: a new scanner can shift the image distribution
All training images came from one scanner type
Validate on labelled images from the new scanner before relying on it

D05.hint: Think about where all the training images came from.

rubric.point: All images come from one hospital and one scanner type
So the team cannot claim the model generalises to other scanners/populations
External validation on another hospital's data is needed
